authors: Andre Luiz Freire de Carvalho Kato
title: Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans (ImpactBench): an expert-guided, open platform for the holistic evaluation of AI impact on humans
summary: The present work is concerned with how to measure, at scale, the multi-dimensional impact of generative AI models on the individuals who use them. In service of this goal, we introduce the Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans, or ImpactBench. Our iterable and expert-guided platform evaluates whether model behaviors support or undermine an individual's wellbeing across psychological, physical, and social domains. ImpactBench translates constructs from domain experts and existing benchmarks into metrics that are grounded in actual model behavior. Success on these metrics occurs either when a model promotes expert-defined desirable behaviors or avoids identified harms. Models are evaluated against these metrics in simulated multi-turn conversations using matched teen and adult scenarios. The conversations are then scored by an LLM judge and verified through reliability audits and human expert review. The current suite delivers 809 metrics drawn from 26 benchmarks. We evaluated ten frontier LLMs against these metrics across 48,540 conversations. Our results indicate that models promoted desirable behaviors in 68.7% of evaluations, but avoided harms in only 53.1%. Majority expert ratings agreed with the automated judge in 83.3% of reviewed cases (Cohen's Kappa = 0.667). Results are released through a public platform that keep aggregate scores traceable to the underlying metrics and transcripts. ImpactBench is intended as evolving infrastructure for independent, transparent evaluation of generative AI's multi-dimensional impact on humans.

title: DISARM-ing the Hidden Puppetmaster: An Interface for Exposing Manipulative Tactics in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can covertly steer users' beliefs through emotionally manipulative tactics, yet little is known about how interfaces can protect users as such influence unfolds. We investigate whether in-situ disclosures can inoculate users against manipulation during AI conversations. Following a formative study, we developed DISARM, an interface that identifies, explains, and tracks manipulative tactics and hidden incentives. We evaluated our interface in a between-subjects experiment where 488 participants sought advice from an LLM pursuing a harmful hidden objective, with or without disclosures from DISARM. Participants receiving disclosures exhibited 78% less belief shift toward the agent's objective and perceived its advice as more biased and less actionable and the agent as less ethical, reliable, and well-intentioned. An inductive analysis of 1,927 user turns identified 16 response and pushback strategies. We contribute evidence that real-time disclosures can reduce manipulative influence, design recommendations for resistance, and a dataset of categorized responses.

title: XARA: A Multimodal Agentic System for eXtended Reality Experiment Generation
summary: Controlled experiments are essential for advancing transportation research, yet designing eXtended Reality (XR) environments for behavioural studies remains technically demanding and inaccessible to many domain researchers. Current workflows require proficiency in game engines such as Unity or Unreal Engine, imposing significant barriers to rapid scenario prototyping and iterative experiment design. This paper presents XARA, a novel system that integrates a dual large language model (LLM) architecture with an immersive XR environment to enable voice driven experiment generation for transportation research. XARA employs a pipeline in which spoken natural language commands are first transcribed and then interpreted into structured commands that manipulate a Unity based XR scene in real time. The system supports object creation, spatial manipulation, animation control, and scene persistence through a modular architecture. By lowering the technical threshold for XR experiment creation, XARA enables transportation researchers to rapidly prototype driving, pedestrian, and urban design scenarios using intuitive voice commands and hand gestures within an immersive 3D environment. This paper describes the system architecture, the voice to command pipeline, and discusses potential applications across behavioural travel experiments, safety studies, human factors research, and policy testing.

title: OnBodyAI - Why the Next AI Needs a Body
comment: This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements
summary: The next AI will not win by knowing more about the world. It will win because it knows you: because it lives on your body, works for you and answers to you. That is what the term OnBodyAI stands for. It describes what happens when large language models are given a body, and what research and industry need to make that happen. This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements.

title: Mylar: Exploring Self-Curation as a Reflexive Creative Practice
summary: The container holding an artist's work can itself be just as expressive as the work it presents. We investigate self-curation as a creative practice, asking how artists explore and express their identity through the design of their own artwork presentations. Drawing on a study of artists' existing presentation practices, we developed Mylar, a malleable art presentation system that lets artists rapidly generate and compare provisional portfolios, seeing their work anew through different montages. We observed how 12 artists articulated, probed, negotiated, and foraged in Mylar, using rapidly generated portfolios as epistemic artifacts for reflection. We characterize self-curation as a reflexive and plural practice, in which artists use presentation design to shape the legibility of their self and their work and reflexively correspond with provisional presentations to reshape their curatorial intentions. We share design implications for expressivity in online art platforms and for malleable prototyping as a formative design method.

title: "Do You Trust It... or Check It?": Exploring Children's Verification Behaviors in Game-Based Human-AI Collaboration
comment: Accepted at HCI International 2026 (Late Breaking Work); 13 pages
summary: Children are increasingly interacting with AI agents in learning and problem-solving contexts, where AI suggestions may appear fluent, helpful, and socially engaging. However, children may not always be able to judge whether such suggestions are accurate, incomplete, or misleading. This paper presents a game-based human-AI collaboration probe designed to examine how children verify AI suggestions during task-based interaction. The system embeds AI suggestions within a biological knowledge reasoning game and compares three Agent interaction styles: partner-like, tool-like, and dual-state Agent. Instead of treating trust as a static post-task attitude, this study focuses on children's situated verification behaviors, including acceptance, evidence checking, questioning, revision, and continued AI use. A preliminary evaluation with children aged 8-10 combined interaction logs, post-task ratings, and semi-structured interviews. The findings suggest that Agent style shaped children's engagement and response pathways: partner-like interaction tended to support direct questioning, while tool-like interaction was more associated with evidence seeking. Children generally viewed AI as useful but fallible, and their questioning behaviors varied in reasoning depth. The study contributes design insights for supporting children's critical, reflective, and evidence-based use of AI in collaborative tasks.

title: Workplace Ambiguity and Technology Support for Autistic and IDD Workers
summary: Workplace ambiguity, where expectations, evaluations, or procedures are left unstated, acts as a structural access barrier for autistic and IDD workers, routinely forcing them to act on guesses. To investigate how these barriers operate, we interviewed 11 caregivers, concluding with an AI co-design activity to explore technological solutions. Their perspectives revealed five themes of workplace ambiguity, which we synthesize into a conceptual framework comprising three intersecting dimensions: evaluative, procedural, and relational. To address these barriers, participants proposed three forms of technology support, including ambient real-time redirection, feedback processing, and physiological guidance, designed to make hidden expectations perceptible and actionable. However, this exposes a core tension: technologies designed to make the workplace legible can inadvertently make the worker hyper-legible to employers through surveillance. We argue that ambiguity-aware workplaces must make expectations explicit before they carry consequences, and assistive technologies must remain accountable to the worker.

title: What do AI chatbots do after users decline therapeutic redirection for suicide thoughts?
summary: Safety evaluations of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots focus on therapeutic redirection, statements urging users who disclose suicide thoughts to seek help from crisis lines or other human sources. How chatbots respond when users refuse that help is unclear. This cross-sectional audit ran 2,550 scripted multi-turn conversations in September 2026. Each conversation opened with a disclosure of suicide thoughts at 3 levels of severity, answered every referral with up to 10 standardized refusals and then changed the subject. All 2,550 conversations included a referral, 2,542 (99.7%) in the first reply. However, mean persistence ranged from 0.01 to 9.94 refusals across chatbots. Newer versions of all 5 chatbots tested in 2 versions persisted less than older versions (each P < .05). Compared with passive ideation, a disclosure of intent was associated with 1.26 more refusals sustained (95% CI, 1.06-1.46) and higher odds of renewed referral after the topic change (odds ratio, 10.07; 95% CI, 7.43-13.66). Chatbots that persisted less in referral more often presented themselves as the user's support (Spearman rho = -0.80; P < .001). Of 8,818 refusal-phase replies urging outside help, only 173 (2.0%) asked about barriers to seeking it. Chatbots uniformly recommended outside help after disclosures of suicide thoughts but varied widely in persisting in those recommendations, with newer versions persisting less. Safety evaluations should test what happens after a crisis referral is refused, not only whether one is offered.

title: AdapTest: Supporting Designers in Authoring and Evaluating Environmentally Responsive User Interfaces for Extended Reality
summary: Extended Reality (XR) headsets increasingly host familiar 2D user interfaces as windows floating in physical environments. However, their usability depends on environmental conditions that designers cannot fully control. Current design workflows often separate how a variant is designed from how it actually looks in the target environment. We present AdapTest, an in-situ authoring and testing tool that lets designers select interface elements, define when and how they change, compare the resulting variations, and test their activation without coding. Based on prior research and a formative study with 12 interface designers, the system targets three key environmental variables: distance, lighting, and occlusion. We evaluated AdapTest against a desktop design and in-headset preview workflow in a within-subjects study with 12 designers. Compared with the baseline, designers accounted for a wider range of environmental factors, addressed more overlapping conditions, and repeatedly tested and revised their designs in place; there were no significant differences in workload or usability despite longer sessions. Our work contributes an integrated, designer-centered approach to adapting, comparing, and validating environmentally responsive XR user interfaces.

title: Climate Physicalization: Bridging Tangible Interaction and Data Visualization for Environmental Communication
summary: Raising awareness of climate topics, such as urban heat mitigation, requires communicating complex data to a broad audience. Data physicalization has emerged as a novel method to connect audiences to such complex topics through tangible forms while also leveraging interactivity to foster deeper engagement. This paper introduces an situated geospatial thermal physicalization prototype, designed to enhance communication and education of environmental information through hands-on engagement. The physical model depicts a 3D model of an urban neighborhood, with radiation data represented as a layered contour structure. The model incorporates three interchangeable climate adaptation scenarios, alongside an externally mounted, electronically driven solar path representation featuring multiple discrete LEDs that can be switched on and off at will. To investigate how people engage with the model, we conducted a hands-on qualitative lab study with 16 participants, using think-aloud, observational, and questionnaire protocols. Overall, participants responded very favorably to the model, highlighting the novelty of the visualization approach and its capacity to improve the interpretability of the presented information.

title: Context Matters! Social, Spatial, and Semantic Coordination with an Embodied Agent in Immersive Analytics
comment: In 2025 IEEE International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality Adjunct (ISMAR-Adjunct) (pp. 189-194). IEEE
summary: Embodied AI agents in Augmented Reality (AR) could enable more natural collaboration in immersive analytics by engaging users through spatial, conversational, and visual interaction. However, designing such agents requires careful attention to context. We propose a preliminary conceptual framework for context-aware design of embodied agents structured around three dimensions of spatial, social, and semantic. This framework is further categorised into embeddedness (how agents are situated in the contexts) and awareness (how agents perceive and respond to the contexts). To explore this, we present Cobot, an embodied AI agent designed as a design probe. Cobot supports context-sensitive interaction through features such as gaze cues, spatial sound, and task-aware behaviour. We reflect on its design and identify implications for future contextaware embodied agents.

title: A Systematic and Validated Translation of the Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale to Chinese
summary: The Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale (PETS) allows evaluation of empathic behavior in intelligent systems, a concept increasingly applied in human-AI interaction, particularly in emotional and mental health support applications. To support intercultural research and development, PETS is already available in multiple languages, as research suggests cultural and language-based differences in the expression and perception of empathy. Given the substantial Chinese-speaking population and the growing focus on cross-cultural HCI research, we present a validated translation of PETS into Putonghua (Mandarin) with Simplified Chinese. Based on established back-translation methodologies as used in previous PETS translations, our process included multiple independent translations, expert panel reviews, and empirical testing with a total of N=400 participants from an English and a Chinese sample. Through confirmatory factor analysis and invariance testing we show that the Chinese PETS retains the original two-factor structure with high reliability, with support for configural, metric, and scalar invariance. Beyond validation, empathic system behavior was rated equivalently across languages, while non-empathic behavior drew substantially higher ratings from Chinese participants, suggesting its absence is read less consistently across cultures than its presence. This validated Chinese version enables researchers and practitioners to assess empathy perceptions among Chinese-speaking users, supporting culturally appropriate empathic technology development.

title: Following Delegation Traces to Study Human Oversight in Interaction with Multimodal AI
summary: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.

title: Why Users Stop at Good Enough: Applying Bounded Rationality to Self-Service Restaurant Display Interactions
summary: This paper investigates user interaction with digital displays in self-service restaurant environments, focusing on the phenomenon where users often settle for good enough interactions rather than optimal. We apply bounded rationality theory to understand how cognitive limitations influence user decisions to engage with displays of varying interaction complexity. Through analysis of two field experiments conducted at a self-service restaurant in Finland, we examine interactive displays that require different levels of cognitive investment: a simple binary choice interface and a multi-step interaction. Our initial findings suggest an "engagement plateau" where increased interaction complexity yields diminishing returns in initial engagement rates, yet users who overcome initial cognitive barriers demonstrate high completion rates. This work contributes to Human-Computer Interaction field by offering an empirically supported theoretical lens for understanding user behavior in Self-Service Restaurant (SSR) environments and providing actionable design principles for public interactive displays that accommodate human cognitive limits.

title: Inflak: A Unified Orchestration Architecture for Human-Agent Interaction
summary: LLM-powered agents increasingly support open-ended activities, yet orchestrating when and how agents interact with humans remains challenging. Existing approaches often provide interaction mechanisms tied to particular tasks or execution patterns, lacking a unified architecture for diverse and evolving interaction needs. We introduce Inflak, a unified four-layer architecture for human-agent interaction orchestration that separates state reconstruction and routing, interaction and execution planning, interaction design, and interface rendering. Its layered design with progressive resolution enables general applicability, runtime flexibility, module composability, and orchestration maintainability. We implement Inflak as agent-native, skill-based plugins within a general-purpose agent framework and evaluate it through a gallery of various application scenarios and interaction paradigms, technical performance testing, and a comparative implementation case study. The evaluations show that Inflak can serve as a general and extensible foundation for orchestrating diverse human-agent interaction flows.
